$comment: The rule inventory: every rule the harness enforces, and — the point of the file — where each one actually lives. `enforcedBy.kind` is the honest answer to core's own rule that a rule not in schemas/ is not a cafaye rule. `schema` means a JSON Schema constraint decides it. `doc` means a convention document states it and no schema can, so it is in this harness's source. `harness` means the rule is a fact about a filesystem or a pin rather than about a document, and lives in the named function. The set of ids here is asserted equal to RULE_IDS in harness/cafaye_contract.py, and the same set appears as a table in docs/contract-harness.md; three statements of one list, and a core test that they agree. `implementedBy` is not one of the three kinds and is not asserted: it names the function a `doc` rule happens to live in, which is what a reader wants and `kind` alone does not say.

rules.claim: Every postgres image reference a repository makes resolves to the one tag core declares in POSTGRES_TAG, and any repository that needs another one declares it with a reason, an owner and a horizon.
rules.reads: Executable declarations only: an `image:` key in a compose file or a workflow's `services:`, and a `docker run`/`create` line in a shell script. Prose is not a source — a grep over the fleet's history finds six CHANGELOGs naming `postgres:17` and every one of them is correct about when it was written.

rules.claim: Core publishes exactly one readable postgres tag, at POSTGRES_TAG, and it is a tag and not `latest`.
rules.why: Every reference in a service is compared against it, so a core that publishes none leaves the rule with nothing to compare and a run that cannot find what it is checking. A refusal and exit 2, for exactly the reason core.version-absent is one — and `latest` is refused because it is the one value that would make the rule pass precisely the references it exists to fail.

rules.claim: A service's cafaye.yml satisfies core's manifest schema.
A published event type starts with the publishing service's own name.
A service never consumes its own events.
Every consumed event type exists in core's catalog.
Every published event type exists in core's catalog, so a consumer is known to be waiting for it.
Every published event type has a payload schema under schemas/events/.
rules.whyCoupled: Not reachable on its own, and the sentence that used to say why was half wrong. It said "every type in core's catalog has a payload schema — test_every_published_fleet_event_has_a_catalog_row_and_a_payload_schema asserts exactly that", and that test asserts something narrower: it ranges over fleet.yml's `events`, not over the catalog. The catalog deliberately contains nine types no publisher ships (identity's five tenancy events, billing's four), and those owe a schema when their packet lands, so a PUBLISHED type without one is necessarily a type the catalog does not list and the two fire together — which is the reachability fact breakage 8 needs. Publishing another service's type instead trips event.own-prefix and never reaches this rule. self_test.sh breakage 8 asserts both, and it is the only breakage that asserts two rules.

rules.claim: exposes.api resolves to a file inside the service repository.
The OpenAPI document declares 3.1.
info.version is present and is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and moves with the /vN prefix.
The OpenAPI document declares at least one path; an empty set is not a contract.
Every path sits under a /vN prefix.
One /vN per document; a second prefix is a breaking change that must be a decision.
Every non-2xx response declares application/problem+json. A document that defines the problem schema and attaches it to nothing has defined an error body no client receives.
In a problem example, `code` is the last segment of `type`, in snake_case. The two fields are one field written twice, and a client can only read one of them.

A reserved code carries the status core fixes for it. Reserved is a floor and not a ceiling: five of the seven OpenAPI documents in the cafaye workspace use an envelope code outside the nine — billing and courier (bad_request), gateway (invalid_json, account_locked, payload_too_large), identity (those three plus method_not_allowed, service_unavailable) and pantry (method_not_allowed) — and core's own conventions name two more that are not on the list, cursor_expired and gone. errors[].code is not counted and is not reserved: the conventions' own example holds invalid_format there.
The problem schema a response references requires trace_id, because a property that is only declared is optional and an error nobody can trace is an error nobody fixes.

No operation takes an offset, page, page_number, page_no or skip query parameter. An offset skips rows inserted before it, so a client paging a list that is being written to reads a row twice and drops another.
An operation that pages accepts a cursor and answers {"data": [...], "page": {"next_cursor": ..., "has_more": ...}}. `limit` with no cursor is the half-adopted case and is reported too.

Every mutating POST accepts an Idempotency-Key header parameter. The strict reading of "that can be retried safely": a document cannot say a POST is unsafe to retry, and inventing an x- extension to let it would be a contract change.
A POST that accepts Idempotency-Key declares the 409 it returns when a key is replayed with a different body. A `default` is not accepted: it hides the path rather than describing it.
A service's declared `core:` constraint admits the version core publishes.
A `core:` constraint is in the grammar the resolver accepts, and a `core:` field is present and is a string.
core's contract surface digests to the sha256 the consumer pinned, when the consumer pins one.
Core publishes exactly one readable version, so a `core:` constraint is resolvable at all.
The directory named by --core is a cafaye/core checkout, not merely a directory.
The run names where it looked for core. It never skips and exits 0.
The service root carries a cafaye.yml. An empty report's OK is not a pass.
A YAML construct outside the declared subset is refused with a file and a line, never guessed.
An SLO declaration satisfies core's SLO schema: the 28-day period, an objective that is never 100, a required description and runbook, and the two alert switches the tier alone derives.
Both SLI queries carry the literal {{.window}} token, which Sloth substitutes with each burn-rate window.
Every metric in an SLI query is one core's SLI catalogue names.
No unbounded dimension — tenant, user_id, account_id, request_id — appears in an SLI query or in one of its labels.
rules.whyCoupled: One scan, two lists, two reasons — and the reason is what a reader is owed at the moment they are about to add one. They share `_denylisted` and are deliberately NOT one rule: unbounded dimensions are barred on the 2000-combination-cap grounds metrics.schema.json already established, and infrastructure signals are barred because an SLO on them is not an SLO on behaviour. Merging them keeps the enforcement and loses the second reason. The self-test breaks both, because a rule whose reason is shared with another is a rule whose breakage could quietly depend on it.

rules.claim: No infrastructure signal — cpu, memory, pod, restart — appears in an SLI query or in one of its labels.
Each SLI query is exactly the composition of the catalogue entry it names, for this service's labels.
No SLO declaration carries a burn-rate catalog of its own; the windows are pinned once, in core.
No two SLOs in a service share a name, across files as well as within one.

warningsComment: Things the harness did NOT check, which is a different sentence from things it checked and found acceptable. A warning never reaches Result.exit_code: seven of the thirteen repositories in the cafaye workspace declare no exposes.api, so an enforced rule over the OpenAPI document would turn seven of them red the moment core updated, which is how a fleet stops running a check. These ids are asserted equal to WARNING_IDS in harness/cafaye_contract.py by `_check_inventory_declares`, which refuses rather than warns — an inventory that has drifted from the code is the same defect as a schema that has drifted from its examples. Deliberately NOT in `rules` above and deliberately not in docs/contract-harness.md's rule table: a list that mixed the two would make "the rules that gate" describe something else.

warnings.claim: The manifest declares no exposes.api, so no openapi.* rule ran. That is not a pass over the document; it is no document.
A document is checked in beside the manifest that exposes.api does not name, so every openapi.* rule skipped it. gateway is the one in the cafaye workspace today.
A $ref that is not a local pointer, which the harness cannot read: it reads a checkout of core and never fetches a file. Whatever is behind that pointer was not checked, and no rule claims otherwise.
A compose-shaped file sits below the two-level depth compose.postgres-pin scans, so nothing in it was read.
warnings.why: The bound exists so the walk does not enter node_modules, and courier vendors hex packages into deps/ where a third-party README documents postgres. A bound that could hide a pin is the same defect as a checker that finds nothing and reports success, so a file outside the bound is named rather than passed over. The harness could not have been left silent here.

notEnforced.claim: A live response validates against the event envelope and the per-type payload schema.
notEnforced.why: A contract test in PLAN.md §3's sense: it needs a running service, and core ships no runtime. darkroom's tests/contract.rs names this as what `caf contract test` was supposed to do. Still owed.

notEnforced.claim: Every service declares at least one SLO, and a `critical` or `high` one has a runbook that exists.
notEnforced.why: The harness validates the SLOs a service DECLARES: it reads `slos/*.yaml`, and a repository with no `slos/` directory is a repository that declares nothing, so it is checked on no SLO rules and passes. That is the same shape as `worker-only.cafaye.yml` declaring no `exposes.api`, and it is recorded here rather than treated as a pass over something. Nothing in the fleet declares an SLO yet — the metrics the catalogue names do not all exist — so making the directory mandatory would turn every service in the workspace red on a rule they cannot yet satisfy. It becomes enforceable the moment the first real SLO lands; until then it is written down.

notEnforced.claim: An SLI's PromQL is syntactically valid, not merely the canonical text.
notEnforced.why: PromQL parsing is `sloth validate`'s job, and Sloth is a Go binary this repository does not carry: taking it would mean core's gate reaching the network for a tool on a runner that may be air-gapped. `check_slo_sli_is_canonical` compares each query against the canonical composition as a string, which is stricter about the SHAPE and blinder about the GRAMMAR. docs/slo.md gives the pinned command for a service that has network, and DECISIONS.md D28 records the choice. Not skipped for inconvenience — the shape is checked, and the one thing left is named.

notEnforced.claim: The `core:` constraint is satisfied by a release inside the range.
notEnforced.why: core publishes no machine-readable spec version, so there is nothing on either side of the comparison. Publishing one is a core change and is listed in docs/contract-harness.md as owed.

notEnforced.claim: The OpenAPI document agrees with the service's router.
notEnforced.why: It needs the service's language: courier reads `Router.__routes__/0` in ExUnit, muse compares against a live FastAPI app. That is a per-language test and cannot be a language-neutral harness, which is why courier's own test stays. The half that IS decidable from a document alone — the reserved error codes, the problem+json envelope, the pagination envelope and the idempotency header — is enforced by eight rules in the harness, and this entry is the other half, which is not.

notEnforced.claim: Every reserved error code is used by the service, and no error path exists that the document never declared.
notEnforced.why: Both halves need the implementation rather than the document. Which codes a service *reaches* is a fact about its code, and whether it has an undocumented failure path is the document-vs-router question the entry above already declines. Worse, a document that declares no non-2xx response at all passes all eight error rules vacuously — the same two-empty-sets shape `openapi.has-paths` exists for, and `openapi.has-paths` is only enforced because core-13 argued for it against an existing fixture. Requiring every operation to declare a failure path is a manager's call about what a service's document has to contain, and until it is made the ceiling is written down rather than enforced.

Readable, but only from an example, and a document that carries no examples has stated nothing this could check — so the rule's answer would depend on how much prose an author happened to write. The stronger half of the same paragraph, that a reserved code carries its fixed status, is enforced from the same examples; this half would add a rule whose firing depends on the absence of a fixture rather than on a defect.

3.1 spells it `type: [string, "null"]` and 3.0 spells it `nullable: true`, and courier's 3.1 document uses the second. Deciding it inside the pagination rule would accuse a document of a pagination mistake for a versioning one, and a 3.1 document containing 3.0 spelling is a real finding that belongs to a dialect rule about `nullable`, which this packet is not and which `openapi.document-is-31` does not currently cover.

notEnforced.claim: format: uri is asserted by core's own suite.
notEnforced.why: jsonschema registers no uri checker without rfc3987-validator, so the assertion in schemas/telemetry/otel-endpoint.schema.json is vacuous in `bin/prime`. The harness checks it, which is what made the gap visible. See D22.

notEnforced.claim: Prose that names a postgres image is checked.
notEnforced.why: A grep over the fleet's own history finds `postgres:17` in six CHANGELOGs, `postgres:18-alpine` in muse's, and `postgres:16-alpine` in two of the docs repository's runbooks — every one a correct statement about what was true when it was written. A rule that read prose would turn six changelogs red for being accurate, and the fix a service owner reaches for is deleting the record, which is strictly worse than the drift it was meant to catch. The rule reads executable declarations, where an `image:` key is the anchor that makes a line a declaration and the repository name excludes redis, nats, grafana and a service's own build image.

notEnforced.claim: A third-party postgres — pgvector, a private mirror, postgres-backup — is the fleet image.
notEnforced.why: It is a different image with a different maintainer, and the platform decision is about the official one. `docker.io/library/postgres` and `ghcr.io/anyone/postgres` ARE recognised as it, because they are it: the repository name is the discriminator, and `postgres-backup` and `pgvector` fail it. Measured: zero in the fleet.

notEnforced.claim: The postgres pin is checked in every repository that runs a database.
notEnforced.why: The rule reads a repository's OWN files, and it refuses to walk into a dependency directory, follow a symlink, or recurse without a bound. So a compose file below COMPOSE_SCAN_DEPTH is not read — and the harness says so in a WARN rather than passing over it in silence. `courier` vendors hex packages into `deps/`, one of which documents postgres in a README, and a walk that read that would be reading a third party's prose as this repository's pin. `extends:` and `include:` are the same shape: an image reached through a pointer to another file is a file the harness was not pointed at, and pointing it is a one-line change.
